title: Rapid Cavity-Based Mid-Circuit Measurement and Feedforward in a Neutral Atom Array
authors: Tsai-Chen Lee, Jacquelyn Ho, Yue-Hui Lu, Tai Xiang, Nathaniel B. Vilas, Zhenjie Yan, Dan M. Stamper-Kurn
abstract: Measuring part of a quantum system in the midst of its evolution and acting on the result in real time is essential for numerous quantum information protocols. Neutral-atom arrays are a leading platform for quantum information processing, but their mid-circuit measurement-and-feedforward cycle times have remained slow, typically exceeding 1 ms. Here we demonstrate fast mid-circuit measurement and real-time feedforward in an array of atomic qubits coupled to a high-finesse optical cavity. Local light shifts tune individual data qubits out of resonance with the cavity, shielding their coherence, while a near-resonant probe drives a selected qubit whose emission is collected with Purcell enhancement. Mid-circuit measurements of four qubits with sub percent infidelity reduce the coherence of a fifth unmeasured data qubit by less than 2%. We implement real-time feedforward to correct measurement-induced phase shifts and to realize an adaptive circuit for optimal quantum state discrimination and conditional state preparation. Our approach reduces the measurement-and-feedforward cycle time to below 100 $μ$s and establishes optical cavities as a route to fast control of neutral-atom quantum systems.
summary: The research demonstrates fast mid-circuit measurement and feedforward control in an array of neutral atoms coupled to an optical cavity. By utilizing site-selective light shifts, they reduced the operational cycle time from milliseconds to microseconds while maintaining high fidelity. This breakthrough establishes a powerful tool for implementing complex quantum algorithms on atomic qubits.
main_problem: The core challenge is achieving fast, high-fidelity mid-circuit measurement and real-time feedforward control necessary for advanced quantum information protocols.
main_result: The authors demonstrated a significant speedup, reducing the measurement-and-feedforward cycle time to below 100 $\mu$s, establishing optical cavities as a viable route for fast control in neutral atom arrays.
method: They employ site-selective illumination using near-resonant probe beams and coherence-shielding light shifts on neutral atoms trapped in an array coupled to a high-finesse optical cavity.
model_or_system: The platform is a neutral atom array (using $^{87}	ext{Rb}$) acting as qubits, interrogated via cavity Quantum Electrodynamics (QED) interactions. Control relies on precisely tuned light shifts and real-time classical feedback processing measurement outcomes.
key_observables: Detection infidelity ($\le 1\%$), coherence reduction on unmeasured qubits ($\le 2\%$), and the cycle time ($< 100 \mu$s).
important_parameters: Cavity coupling strength, probe/shielding detunings, measurement duration (optimized to $\sim 7-30 \mu$s), and feedback loop latency.
main_assumptions: The shielding mechanism is modeled using Hamiltonian diagonalization; the analysis assumes minimal crosstalk between neighboring sites during measurement.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental setup, Ramsey measurements showing fidelity improvement with feedforward correction, and comparisons of state discrimination success probabilities between fixed and adaptive measurement schemes.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the fundamental speedup via cavity coupling to demonstrating its application in complex tasks like Ramsey sequence fidelity enhancement, culminating in benchmarking optimal adaptive control for quantum state discrimination and preparation.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses a major bottleneck—the measurement latency—in solid-state and neutral atom quantum computing architectures by integrating high-speed optical readout with real-time classical feedback.
